label: explain-track-4
one_line: We will print 21 spinning seed models, drop them in water, and test whether a published model or a simple rule predicts how fast they sink.
what: Some trees make fruit with two curved wings. The fruit spins like a helicopter blade as it falls. Researchers 3D-printed copies and dropped them in a tall tank of water. We want to write our guesses down first, then print 21 new shapes and drop them. We have two guesses to compare. One is a published computer model that cuts each wing into thin strips. The other is a much simpler rule that the earlier designer built. The test measures how fast each model sinks. It does not measure sideways gliding. So far this is a plan with no new results.
why: Spinning fruit fall slowly, so wind can carry the seeds away from the parent tree. If we can predict the best wing curve, we learn how a simple shape gets good flight. Our project also keeps a list of checked rules about gliding. This test shows whether a published model holds up when we call the result in advance. A miss would be useful too. We make no claim that it will help medicine or machines yet.

steps.text: Download the public data and the model code from the research group. Both are free to reuse under the MIT licence.
steps.picture: Borrowing a recipe book that the cook says anyone may copy.

steps.text: Re-do the earlier arithmetic from scratch. Every number we checked came out the same, apart from tiny rounding.
steps.picture: Adding up a restaurant bill a second time and getting the same total.

steps.text: Write down what the model predicts for each of 21 new wing shapes. Seal the file before any drop happens.
steps.picture: Calling the score before the match starts.

steps.text: Write down what the simple rival rule predicts for the same shapes. It is the earlier designer's own rule, not a proven law.
steps.picture: Asking a second friend to guess the score too.

steps.text: Print the 21 shapes. Each differs in how much the wings are curved and how the wing root is tilted.
steps.picture: Baking 21 loaves, each with a slightly different shape.

steps.text: Drop each one in a tall water tank and time its steady sinking speed. Repeat the drops, because print-to-print scatter is a few percent.
steps.picture: Dropping the same stone many times to see how much the timing wobbles.

steps.text: Compare the sealed guesses with the measured speeds. Count a win only when the gap is bigger than the scatter.
steps.picture: Two runners are only separate if they finish further apart than the stopwatch error.

steps.text: Publish the result, including a miss. Also plan a second test with a flat plate that really glides sideways.
steps.picture: Telling the team both the wins and the flops.

wrong_if: Our bet, written before looking: the model should pick the right wing curve and the right order of speeds for the tilted-root shapes. If it misses by more than the print-to-print scatter, it is wrong. If the simple rule does as well, the strip model adds nothing. Public data already hint at this. A rule fitted to ten sets of earlier data gave a smaller average error than the model (0.055 against 0.088 in log terms). Those were fits to old data, not new calls.
could_go_wrong: The test measures sinking speed, not sideways gliding, so our glide-distance rule does not apply to it.
The published model is partly tuned: its drag was reduced and its weight set to 1.2 grams, so it was not a pure prediction.
Print-to-print scatter of a few percent can make a close contest end in a tie.
The simple rival rule is the earlier designer's own construction, so it may be a weak or unfair opponent.
At a root tilt of 15 degrees the model and the rival differ by only about 6.5 percent, close to the gap between two repeat series at zero tilt (about 7 percent).
The published experiments used only two tilts, 0 and 35 degrees, so 15 degrees has no data at all.
One planned comparison may be unable to fail at all, which would make it useless as evidence.
The public data could change if the repository owner updates it.

questions.q: How do you know the earlier numbers are right?
questions.a: We re-downloaded the files, checked their fingerprints, and re-ran the sums. Results matched, apart from tiny rounding. That shows the numbers were read correctly. It does not show the physics idea is right.

We have not printed or dropped a single new fruit. We have not tested a tilt of 15 degrees in water. We did not re-run every simulation the reviewers used, and some of the test design files we could not find.

questions.q: Why drop things in water instead of air?
questions.a: The researchers used a tall tank of water because the flow there behaves like fast air around a larger seed. The water makes the fall slow enough to measure.
No. A spinning fruit sinks nearly straight down. Our rule for glide distance gives zero for it, so it says nothing here. That is why a flat-plate glider test is suggested alongside.

questions.q: Do real fruits match the best curve?
questions.a: Partly. Wild fruits had an average fold value of 1.8, with about 10 percent measurement error, over 27 fruits. That sits near the model's best value for one tilt. The tilt of each real fruit was not reported.

questions.q: Does wind carry real fruit as far as a simple sum says?
questions.a: No. A simple wind-drift sum came out about 4 to 8 times too far (middle value about 7) for twelve tropical fruit species. Real fruits land much closer to the tree.

questions.q: Why does the glide rule matter at all?
questions.a: Our rule library caps glide distance from a known gliding ratio. We added a checked rule linking that ratio to wing shape: long, thin wings glide further, but only up to a limit. It assumes a standard simple drag model, so it is a limit, not a measurement.

questions.q: Who disagrees on why spinning seeds fall slowly?
questions.a: One account says a small whirl of air stuck to the wing adds lift. The other fits a simple curve to measurements. The chosen model uses the curve, not the whirl.

glossary.plain: Made by a machine that builds a shape from plastic, layer by layer.
A set of sums on a computer that guesses what will happen.

glossary.term: computer model that cuts each wing into thin strips
glossary.plain: A method that adds up the push of air on many thin slices of a wing.
A short formula with one adjustable number that guesses the sinking speed.
The simple rule we compare against the strip model.
The angle at which the wing meets the body of the fruit.
A number that says how strongly the wing is curved.
The small differences between copies of the same shape.
How far a glider travels forward for each unit of height it drops.
The push of air or water that slows a moving thing.
The push that holds a wing up or sideways against its fall.
A small tornado of air that clings to the front edge of a wing.
A way to measure how far off a guess is, by ratio rather than by plain difference.
Adjusted after the fact so the numbers match old data.
A permission that lets anyone reuse the files for free.
Guesses saved before the test so they cannot be changed afterwards.
A short code that changes if even one byte of a file changes.
A program that checks a maths proof line by line.
Our list of rules a design must obey, each backed by a checked proof.
A flat sheet with a weight at the front that flutters, glides or dives.
Fruit gathered from trees outside the lab.
A second round of drops with the same shape.
The tall water container the drops happen in.
The constant speed a fruit reaches once it stops speeding up.

check_yourself.what: Re-run the analysis on the downloaded public data.
check_yourself.expect: Output equal to expected_output.txt, for example speed 0.0676, ratio 1.495, lowest Reynolds number 4352 at fold value 1.805.

check_yourself.what: Dump measured speeds and compute the ratio between 0 and 35 degree tilts.
check_yourself.expect: Rows with speeds 0.1011 and 0.0676 metres per second, and a ratio of about 1.496.

check_yourself.what: Check the new maths proof about wing shape and glide ratio.
check_yourself.expect: errors=0 sorryAx=0 and the line ALL CHECKED: no errors, no sorryAx.
A glide ratio of 3.77 at 0.220 chord and 14.9 degrees, and no balance point at 0.30.

check_yourself.expect: 3065098 bytes, sha256 starting c9c2d661, unless the repository has changed.

left_out: Claim that the frozen test is inconclusive about 84 percent of the time if the strip model is true: it comes from the agent's own simulation with assumed scatter, which the checker could not re-run.
Claim that one comparison cannot fail as written: the rule text lives in a design file the checker could not find, so it is left out as fact.
Claim that the model's tilt ratio is 1.22 against 1.50 measured: the 1.22 is only an earlier agent's own number that the checker did not recompute.
Claim that 1.2 grams versus 2.16 grams and a halved drag are exact: the paper only says drag was reduced, so no exact factor is stated.
Claim that the zero glide range for a vertical sinker is a fact of the rule: the zero is the agent's own assumption, so it is stated only as our reading.
The 0.33 to 0.57 expected band for the strip model: it rests on the agent's own assumptions about lead density and key mass.
